items.stem: "I did not understand, then ... I understand it now" shows:
items.answer: reflection by the narrating self
items.markingKey: reflection by the narrating self. The older self interprets the past.

items.stem: Explain why reflection is essential in memoir and personal essays.
items.answer: Without reflection, a memoir is just a sequence of events; reflection shows what the experience meant and why it matters to readers.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Without reflection, a memoir is just a sequence of events; reflection shows what the experience meant and why it matters to readers. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the following memoir extract by a writer remembering her first day in a new country.

I was nine when we arrived in Oslo in January. I had never seen snow, and I had never been so cold that my teeth hurt.
My mother bought me a red coat from a charity shop. It was two sizes too big. 'You will grow into it,' she said, and she was right, though not in the way she meant.
That coat went everywhere with me – to my first Norwegian lesson, to my first sleepover, to the school where nobody could say my name.
I still have it. It fits now. So does the city.

Identify the technique used in "a red coat from a charity shop. It was two sizes too big." and explain its effect.
items.answer: Symbolism: "a red coat from a charity shop. It was two sizes too big." – the oversized coat symbolises the new life that she had to grow into.
items.markingKey: Symbolism: "a red coat from a charity shop. It was two sizes too big." – the oversized coat symbolises the new life that she had to grow into. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a memoir about the writer's grandfather.

My grandfather's tailor's shop in Leicester smelled of steam and chalk. I spent every Saturday of my childhood under his cutting table, collecting the coloured threads that fell like slow rain.
He measured everyone the same way: the bus driver, the bride, the man who came in once a year to have his only suit taken in a little further.
I did not understand, then, that he was measuring the whole neighbourhood – its weddings, its funerals, its slow thinning. I understand it now, every time I sew on a button and get it wrong.

How does the writer use reflection to give meaning to the experience?
items.answer: Memoir conventions: a first-person adult narrator recalls real childhood experiences; specific sensory details ("steam and chalk"); a focus on a relationship; and reflection that interprets the past ("I did not understand, then ... I understand it now").
items.markingKey: Memoir conventions: a first-person adult narrator recalls real childhood experiences; specific sensory details ("steam and chalk"); a focus on a relationship; and reflection that interprets the past ("I did not understand, then ... I understand it now"). Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Identify two memoir conventions in the tailor's shop extract, with evidence.
items.answer: Sensory detail ("steam and chalk"); reflection ("I did not understand, then ... I understand it now"); focus on a relationship (grandfather); first-person adult narrator.
items.markingKey: Sensory detail ("steam and chalk"); reflection ("I did not understand, then ... I understand it now"); focus on a relationship (grandfather); first-person adult narrator.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Memoirs are less truthful than biographies."
items.answer: Memoirs offer subjective, emotional truth rather than objective record; both forms interpret the past.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: memory is selective and biased; writers shape events for meaning. Arguments against: memoirs reveal emotional truth; biographies also interpret evidence. Supported judgement: Memoirs offer subjective, emotional truth rather than objective record; both forms interpret the past.

items.stem:
Read the following text.

I was twelve the summer my father stopped going to the yard, though nobody used the word "redundant" in our house. He said he was "between ships".
Every morning he still put on his work boots. He walked me to the bus stop, then kept walking – to the river, I found out later, where he stood for hours watching the empty cranes.
I thought he was the bravest man in the world. I know now that bravery and pride can look exactly the same from the height of a twelve-year-old.

This text is best classified as a:
items.answer: novel extract
items.markingKey: B. It is a novel extract: it uses conventions such as a narrator, characters, setting and plot, developed through description, dialogue and inner thoughts.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a travel blog about the Atacama Desert, Chile.

At four in the morning, in the driest desert on Earth, I lay on a frozen ground sheet and watched the Milky Way rise like smoke from behind the volcano.
Our guide, Rodrigo, whose grandmother herded llamas on these salt flats, pointed out the dark shapes between the stars. "Other people see constellations," he said. "My people saw a llama, a fox, a toad – in the dark spaces."
I have looked at the night sky my whole life. That night was the first time I had been taught how to see it.

How would you describe the writer's tone? Refer to two language choices that create it.
items.answer: The tone is awed and humble: wonder at the sky and respect for Rodrigo create an awed, humble tone.
items.markingKey: The tone is awed and humble: wonder at the sky and respect for Rodrigo create an awed, humble tone. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Lukas writes: "Memoir must include every detail exactly as it happened." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Memoir selects and shapes memories for meaning; writers should be honest but cannot recall everything exactly.
items.markingKey: Memoir selects and shapes memories for meaning; writers should be honest but cannot recall everything exactly. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Rewrite this flat sentence with a sensory detail and a reflection: "I used to visit my aunt's farm every summer."
items.answer: E.g. "Every summer I woke at my aunt's farm to the smell of hay and diesel; only later did I realise those weeks were the only time my mother laughed." Credit sense detail and reflection.
items.markingKey: E.g. "Every summer I woke at my aunt's farm to the smell of hay and diesel; only later did I realise those weeks were the only time my mother laughed." Credit sense detail and reflection.

items.answer: a superlative

items.stem: Explain the difference between exoticism and respectful representation.
items.answer: Exoticism makes a place seem strange and timeless for outsiders; respectful representation shows it as complex and modern, with local voices.

items.stem:
Read the following travel blog post by a 15-year-old visiting Iceland.

Day 4: I Stood Next to a Volcano (and Lived)
Posted by @nadia_explores
OK, so technically the eruption at Fagradalsfjall had stopped. But the ground was still breathing. Steam curled out of black rock like the earth was exhaling after a long run.
Our guide, Sigga, said the lava field was younger than me. I didn't know rocks could be younger than me!!
My boots smelled of sulphur (rotten eggs, basically) for two days. Worth it.
Drop a 🌋 in the comments if Iceland is on your list!

Outline the purpose of the text and one way in which the writer pursues it.
items.answer: To entertain and share a personal travel experience, and to build a community of followers. Supporting evidence: "I Stood Next to a Volcano (and Lived)" (hyperbolic title) – the exaggerated danger hooks readers while the brackets hint at the joke.
items.markingKey: To entertain and share a personal travel experience, and to build a community of followers. Supporting evidence: "I Stood Next to a Volcano (and Lived)" (hyperbolic title) – the exaggerated danger hooks readers while the brackets hint at the joke. items.answer: Travel writing also reflects on culture, people, the writer's perspective and questions of representation.

items.stem: Analyse how a travel writer you have studied represents a place and its people.
items.answer: Indicative content: sensory description; representation of people; local voices; stereotypes challenged or reinforced; the writer's perspective and reflection. Criteria A and B.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: sensory description; representation of people; local voices; stereotypes challenged or reinforced; the writer's perspective and reflection. Criteria A and B.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Non-fiction that describes places and the writer's experiences of them"?
items.answer: travel writing
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of travel writing.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a travel article about Hanoi, Vietnam.

The guidebook had promised me "timeless Old Quarter charm". What I found at seven in the morning was Mrs Thu, who has sold phở from the same corner for thirty-one years, scrolling the football scores on her phone while her broth simmered.
I had come looking for an unchanging, exotic past. Hanoi was busy being a modern city, and it was not waiting for me.
Mrs Thu handed me a bowl and a pair of chopsticks. "Too much photo," she said, nodding at my camera. "Eat first." She was right.

How does the writer represent the place and its people?
items.answer: Representation of place and culture: the writer questions the guidebook's clichéd image ("timeless ... charm") and the tourist's wish for an "exotic past", presenting Hanoi instead as a modern city and Mrs Thu as a named individual with her own voice and authority.
items.markingKey: Representation of place and culture: the writer questions the guidebook's clichéd image ("timeless ... charm") and the tourist's wish for an "exotic past", presenting Hanoi instead as a modern city and Mrs Thu as a named individual with her own voice and authority. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Identify two ways the Atacama extract gives authority to local knowledge.

items.stem: "Travel writers can never represent another culture fairly." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Perfect representation is impossible, but self-awareness, specificity and local voices allow fair, respectful travel writing.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: outsiders bring biases; short visits give partial views. Arguments against: honest reflection and local voices help; outsiders can notice what insiders take for granted. Supported judgement: Perfect representation is impossible, but self-awareness, specificity and local voices allow fair, respectful travel writing. A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. items.stem: Plan a reflective personal piece in three parts about a moment you changed your mind about someone.

items.stem:
Read the following diary entry by a 13-year-old on a school expedition in the Scottish Highlands.

Wednesday 14 May
Today was the WORST and maybe the BEST day of my life.
We walked 18 km in the rain. My boots filled with water like two buckets. Leo's map blew into a loch. We argued for twenty minutes about which way was north.
Then the clouds split open and there it was: the whole valley, gold and green, with a rainbow sitting on it like a crown.
Nobody said anything for ages. Even Leo stopped complaining.
Tomorrow: 22 km. Help.

Explain how the date and first-person present reflection contributes to the meaning of the text.
items.answer: The date and first-person present reflection: they show the diary's private, immediate voice.
items.markingKey: The date and first-person present reflection: they show the diary's private, immediate voice. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a personal essay by a young writer.

For most of my life, my name has been the hardest word I know.
"Th-" I would begin, and the room would wait, and the wait would fill with kind faces trying not to look kind. Teachers finished my sentences. Friends ordered for me.
At fifteen I joined the debate club, mostly by accident. The first time I spoke, I stammered for eleven seconds – I know, because someone timed it.
Then I finished my argument. We won.
I still stammer. I have simply stopped apologising for the time it takes me to be heard.

Write a personal essay (about 400 words) about a moment when you had to find your voice. End with a reflection that connects your experience to a wider idea.
items.answer: Indicative content: first-person reflective voice; a specific, vividly told moment; honest detail; a structure that moves from experience to insight; a concluding reflection on a wider idea; controlled, varied style.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: first-person reflective voice; a specific, vividly told moment; honest detail; a structure that moves from experience to insight; a concluding reflection on a wider idea; controlled, varied style. Indicative content above. Mark against criteria B, C and D: purpose and audience addressed (C), conventions of the form and logical organisation (B), register, vocabulary and accuracy (D).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "memoir"?
options: A candid voice that admits mistakes, doubts and complex feelings
The way outsiders look at and judge a place according to their own expectations
Writing that explores an experience and what the writer learned from it
A non-fiction account of the writer's own experiences, focused on particular memories and their meaning
items.answer: A non-fiction account of the writer's own experiences, focused on particular memories and their meaning
items.markingKey: D. "memoir" is a non-fiction account of the writer's own experiences, focused on particular memories and their meaning.

items.answer: Memoir focuses on selected experiences and their meaning; autobiography covers the writer's life more fully and chronologically.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "narrating self / experiencing self".
items.answer: The older writer telling the story and the younger self who lived it
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the older writer telling the story and the younger self who lived it. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "representation of place"?
options: A candid voice that admits mistakes, doubts and complex feelings
The writer's thoughtful interpretation of what an experience meant
A short, vivid personal story used to illustrate a point
How a text portrays a place and its people
items.answer: How a text portrays a place and its people
items.markingKey: D. "representation of place" is how a text portrays a place and its people.

items.stem: Explain why reflective pieces need specific moments rather than general summaries.
items.answer: Specific moments let readers experience events and make reflection earned and convincing.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Specific moments let readers experience events and make reflection earned and convincing. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between memoir and autobiography.
items.answer: Memoir focuses on selected experiences and their meaning; autobiography covers the writer's life more fully and chronologically.
items.markingKey: Memoir focuses on selected experiences and their meaning; autobiography covers the writer's life more fully and chronologically. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why travel writers should be careful about stereotypes.
items.answer: Stereotypes reduce people and places to clichés, misinform readers and can be disrespectful.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Stereotypes reduce people and places to clichés, misinform readers and can be disrespectful. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between recounting and reflecting.
items.answer: Recounting tells what happened; reflecting explores what it meant and why it matters.
items.markingKey: Recounting tells what happened; reflecting explores what it meant and why it matters. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why memoirists are not simply objective reporters of the past.
items.answer: Memory is selective and shaped by later understanding, so memoir is an interpretation, not a record.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Memory is selective and shaped by later understanding, so memoir is an interpretation, not a record. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Rewrite this exoticising sentence to represent the place respectfully: "The mysterious natives of the old market haggled in strange tongues."
items.answer: E.g. "In the market, Mr Okafor and his daughter sold yams and joked with customers in Igbo and English." Credit specific, named people and non-exoticising language.
items.markingKey: E.g. "In the market, Mr Okafor and his daughter sold yams and joked with customers in Igbo and English." Credit specific, named people and non-exoticising language.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a memoir about the writer's grandfather.

My grandfather's tailor's shop in Leicester smelled of steam and chalk. I spent every Saturday of my childhood under his cutting table, collecting the coloured threads that fell like slow rain.
He measured everyone the same way: the bus driver, the bride, the man who came in once a year to have his only suit taken in a little further.
I did not understand, then, that he was measuring the whole neighbourhood – its weddings, its funerals, its slow thinning. I understand it now, every time I sew on a button and get it wrong.

Explain how the writer turns a personal experience into a wider reflection, then write a reflective final sentence for a piece of your own on a similar experience.
items.answer: Reflection: the narrator realises that the grandfather's measuring recorded the life of a community; the humble final detail (getting a button wrong) shows lasting love and loss.
items.markingKey: Reflection: the narrator realises that the grandfather's measuring recorded the life of a community; the humble final detail (getting a button wrong) shows lasting love and loss. Indicative content above. Mark against criteria B, C and D: purpose and audience addressed (C), conventions of the form and logical organisation (B), register, vocabulary and accuracy (D).

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a personal essay by a young writer.

For most of my life, my name has been the hardest word I know.
"Th-" I would begin, and the room would wait, and the wait would fill with kind faces trying not to look kind. Teachers finished my sentences. Friends ordered for me.
At fifteen I joined the debate club, mostly by accident. The first time I spoke, I stammered for eleven seconds – I know, because someone timed it.
Then I finished my argument. We won.
I still stammer. I have simply stopped apologising for the time it takes me to be heard.

How would you describe the writer's tone? Refer to two language choices that create it.
items.answer: The tone is candid and quietly defiant: honest detail, dry humour and calm statements create a candid, quietly defiant tone.
items.markingKey: The tone is candid and quietly defiant: honest detail, dry humour and calm statements create a candid, quietly defiant tone. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a travel article about Hanoi, Vietnam.

The guidebook had promised me "timeless Old Quarter charm". What I found at seven in the morning was Mrs Thu, who has sold phở from the same corner for thirty-one years, scrolling the football scores on her phone while her broth simmered.
I had come looking for an unchanging, exotic past. Hanoi was busy being a modern city, and it was not waiting for me.
Mrs Thu handed me a bowl and a pair of chopsticks. "Too much photo," she said, nodding at my camera. "Eat first." She was right.

What is the writer trying to achieve in this travel writing extract? Support your answer with evidence.
items.answer: To describe Hanoi while challenging stereotyped, exoticised representations of the city. Supporting evidence: "who has sold phở from the same corner for thirty-one years" (specific detail) – precise details present Mrs Thu as an individual with a history, not as scenery.
items.markingKey: To describe Hanoi while challenging stereotyped, exoticised representations of the city. Supporting evidence: "who has sold phở from the same corner for thirty-one years" (specific detail) – precise details present Mrs Thu as an individual with a history, not as scenery. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

Explain how ending on a present-tense reflection contributes to the meaning of the text.
items.answer: Ending on a present-tense reflection: the final sentence turns the story into a statement of identity and self-acceptance.
items.markingKey: Ending on a present-tense reflection: the final sentence turns the story into a statement of identity and self-acceptance. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Memoirs are less truthful than biographies."
items.answer: Memoirs offer subjective, emotional truth rather than objective record; both forms interpret the past.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: memory is selective and biased; writers shape events for meaning. Arguments against: memoirs reveal emotional truth; biographies also interpret evidence. Supported judgement: Memoirs offer subjective, emotional truth rather than objective record; both forms interpret the past.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a travel article about Hanoi, Vietnam.

The guidebook had promised me "timeless Old Quarter charm". What I found at seven in the morning was Mrs Thu, who has sold phở from the same corner for thirty-one years, scrolling the football scores on her phone while her broth simmered.
I had come looking for an unchanging, exotic past. Hanoi was busy being a modern city, and it was not waiting for me.
Mrs Thu handed me a bowl and a pair of chopsticks. "Too much photo," she said, nodding at my camera. "Eat first." She was right.

Answer the following question in a well-organised response of about 250 words: How does the writer challenge stereotypical representations of Hanoi?
items.answer: The writer sets the guidebook's cliché "timeless Old Quarter charm" against Mrs Thu "scrolling the football scores on her phone", puncturing the stereotype of an unchanging past. He admits his own bias ("I had come looking for an unchanging, exotic past"), and presents Mrs Thu with specific detail (thirty-one years on the same corner) and her own voice ("Too much photo ... Eat first."). The final "She was right" gives the local person authority over the traveller.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The writer sets the guidebook's cliché "timeless Old Quarter charm" against Mrs Thu "scrolling the football scores on her phone", puncturing the stereotype of an unchanging past. He admits his own bias ("I had come looking for an unchanging, exotic past"), and presents Mrs Thu with specific detail (thirty-one years on the same corner) and her own voice ("Too much photo ... Eat first."). The final "She was right" gives the local person authority over the traveller. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling.

items.stem: Write a reflective personal piece (400–600 words) about a place that mattered to you as a child. Use sensory detail, a clear structure and a final reflection.
items.answer: Indicative content: specific sensory memories; narrating vs experiencing self; a turning point or realisation; reflective conclusion with wider significance; varied, accurate language. Criteria B, C, D.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: specific sensory memories; narrating vs experiencing self; a turning point or realisation; reflective conclusion with wider significance; varied, accurate language. Criteria B, C, D.
